title: Entrepreneur background can shape who gets hired and which wage opportunities persist
source_unit: Census Bureau and LinkedIn profile data on entrepreneurs, startup employees, wages, and social-background similarity

observations.period: Startup cohorts and worker outcomes; paper published July 2026; persistence observed at least 20 years

denominator.unit: U.S. entrepreneurs, startups, and employees in linked Census and LinkedIn data; exact public abstract denominator not disclosed

female_employee_share_difference.unit: percentage-point higher female employee share at female-founded startups after industry-by-metro-area-by-cohort controls

black_employee_share_difference.unit: percentage-point corresponding estimate for Black employees

hispanic_employee_share_difference.unit: percentage-point corresponding estimate for Hispanic employees

noncollege_employee_share_difference.unit: percentage-point corresponding estimate for non-college employees

persistence.value: differences remain stable across new firm cohorts and persist at least 20 years

wage_mechanism.value: demand drives the relative differences; new firms pay higher relative wages to workers from backgrounds similar to the entrepreneur

observations.method: Census and LinkedIn profiles linked to worker and wage data; industry-by-metro-area-by-cohort fixed effects estimate background similarity in hiring. An AKM wage research design and group-specific wage decompositions are used to separate labor-demand and labor-supply explanations; a calibrated model assesses reduced entrepreneurship-access barriers.
observations.uncertainty: This is a Census working paper and has not undergone the review and editorial process of an official Census publication. The public abstract does not disclose all linkage, sample, founder-identification, measurement, or selection details. Similarity in founder and worker backgrounds does not by itself distinguish network trust, discrimination, preferences, information, geography, or occupational sorting.
observations.subgroup: Startup employees grouped by gender, race, ethnicity, age, education, and similarity to the entrepreneur; estimates are reported for female, Black, Hispanic, and non-college employees.
observations.counterinterpretation: Founders may recruit from familiar networks because of information, location, shared skills, or worker supply, not only exclusion. Similar-background hiring can coexist with higher relative wages for those workers, and the observed composition does not establish that other groups were rejected or harmed in every firm.

related_sources.claim: The author-posted paper provides additional abstract context on persistence and modeled relative-wage effects; the Census landing page remains the primary source for this record.

boundary: This record adds a founder-background-to-hiring and wage-opportunity pathway. It does not establish discriminatory intent, unequal productivity, firm performance, worker wellbeing, intergenerational mobility, or a complete causal effect of entrepreneurship access.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Census working-paper landing page reviewed; linked Census, LinkedIn, and wage microdata are not retained
